Senses.PreferredTarget: to step down from the seat
Senses.Explanation: To step down (下) from the seat (座): “to step down from the seat.” The phrase occurs 12,306 times in 376 allowlisted texts. In Chan records it is the recurrent narrative close of an ascent-to-the-hall address: a master speaks, shouts, plants or throws down the staff, or remains silent and steps down. The descent can itself answer a public-interview demand, as when Zhaozhou asks Nanquan to speak apart from the four propositions and hundred negations and Nanquan steps down. In the Yaoshan case, Yaoshan ascends the seat, pauses, then steps down without a word; the rector follows and protests that he had promised to preach. The Zen Buddha is repeatedly made to perform the same seat action: the World-Honored One ascends the seat, Mañjuśrī declares that the Teaching King's teaching is thus, and the World-Honored One immediately steps down; in another scene he refuses to preach to the two vehicles and then steps down. A lay questioner can even tell the master, “Please step down,” inside the interview. The corpus also records people pulling one another down from a seat. Formal closure, responsive departure, command, and forcible removal all retain the same concrete seat action.
Senses.Note: Cross-checked 'ascend the seat' (陞座), 'ascend the hall' (上堂), 'then stepped down' (便下座), 'planted the staff' (卓拄杖), and the Buddha seat narratives. The formal closure and physically being pulled from a seat share one concrete action, so item 8 does not warrant a split.

Occurrences.Kwic: 眾集定。文殊白椎曰。諦觀法王法。法王法如是。世尊便下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Five Lamps record makes the World-Honored One's departure from the seat the whole close of this teaching-seat scene.

Occurrences.Kwic: 世尊曰。吾誓不為二乘聲聞人說法。便下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A second distinct Buddha seat narrative: after the reported refusal to preach, the World-Honored One steps down.

Occurrences.Kwic: 良久曰：太平本是將軍致，不許將軍見太平。喝一喝，下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A later lamp-record hall close: after a pause and line, the master gives one shout and steps down.

Occurrences.Kwic: 上首復白槌云：「諦觀法王法，法王法如是。」下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A formal late-record close with the chief seat's declaration immediately before departure.

Occurrences.Kwic: 適鴻雁一群飛過，師云：「過去了也。」便下座。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The master observes geese passing, says 'they have passed,' and immediately steps down.

Occurrences.Kwic: 麻谷拽師下座，麻谷卻坐。師近前云：「不審。」麻谷擬議，師亦拽麻谷下座，師卻坐；
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The ordinary physical construction is preserved for the sense audit: Maku pulls the master down, then the master pulls Maku down.

Occurrences.Kwic: 眾方集山陞座良久便下座歸方丈主隨後問。和尚適來許為眾說法。云何不垂一言
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The raised Yaoshan case: after agreeing to preach, Yaoshan ascends the seat, pauses, steps down, and returns to the abbot's quarters without speaking.

Occurrences.Kwic: 南泉因趙州問離四句絕百非請師道師下座歸方丈
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In a narrated Nanquan–Zhaozhou interview, Nanquan answers the request to speak beyond the four propositions and hundred negations by stepping down and returning to the abbot's quarters.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師擲下拄杖便下座歸方丈
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A teaching-seat close links the action to the staff: the master throws down the staff, steps down, and returns to the abbot's quarters.

Senses.Explanation: Literally “lay down a word,” this means to offer a response phrase when a master raises a case, an encounter (因緣), or a question and calls for an answer. It occurs 889 times across 205 allowlisted texts and names a standard public testing routine. A master orders the assembly to offer responses; participants put forward words or manage a turning phrase; the recurrent recorded verdict is that the responses “do not accord” (不契). In Nanquan's door case, many people offer responses but none accords with Nanquan's meaning. Another senior monk offers ninety-six turns without satisfying the master. When the assembly's responses fail, the master may supply his own final phrase or speak in their place. Dahui likewise reports successive responders failing to accord in Dongshan's saying and an assembly failing in the bamboo-slat case. Verbal “offer a phrase,” agent “one who offered a phrase,” and nominal “the phrase offered” constructions all denote the same response event and product. The Chan deviation is the institutional demand for an on-the-spot phrase to be publicly measured against a raised case; the entry does not infer what makes any response accord.
Senses.Note: This is a corpus-wide Chan public-response term, not master-specific. The former act/result grammar remains one sense. One exact control witness comes from modern scholarly body prose embedded in an allowlisted text and uses the phrase in “wording and choice of characters” (下語用字) while discussing song-lyric prosody. That editorial wording is preserved as corpus provenance, but one modern scholarly sentence is not promoted into a second Zen lexical sense. Compare substitute or alternative response (代語 / 別語), attached comment (著語), verse on an old case (頌古), and appraisal-commentary (評唱).

Occurrences.Kwic: 遂令學眾下語竟有云云師末後下語云慈氏菩薩
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (古尊宿語錄); the assembly is ordered to lay down words on the '(兜率陀天底)' ('the one in Tusita Heaven') presentation, and when they fizzle the master lays down his own capping word (末後下語云) — '(慈氏菩薩)' (Maitreya). Shows both assembly-(下語) and the master's own.

Occurrences.Kwic: 多有人下語並不契泉意
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (古尊宿語錄), in the episode of Nanquan shutting his quarters' door and ringing it with ash (南泉掩方丈門／灰圍) in the Recorded Sayings of Zhaozhou (趙州諗禪師語錄): Nanquan shuts the door, rings it with ash, and challenges 'say it and I open the door' (南泉便掩却方丈門便把灰圍却問僧云道得即開門…); Zhaozhou cries (蒼天蒼天) ('blue heavens! blue heavens!') and Nanquan opens the door. Many people lay down words, none accord with Nanquan's meaning (不契泉意) — the stock (下語)/(不契) ('lay down a word' / 'does not accord') dynamic.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師令眾下語眾下語畢師復舉
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (普濟玉琳國師語錄); the master orders the assembly to lay down words, and when the laying-down is finished (下語畢) raises the case again — a bare description of the routine.

Occurrences.Kwic: 有一上座下語九十六轉不愜師意
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (傳燈玉英集) (lamp-record digest); a senior monk lays down words through ninety-six turns without satisfying the master (不愜師意) — the testing/failing use.

Occurrences.Kwic: 是日緇素下語頗多師復自代云
Occurrences.AttributionNote: (普濟玉琳國師語錄); that day monks and laity laid down quite a few words, so the master again capped in their stead (自代云) — the master's substitute (下語).

Occurrences.Kwic: 洞山和尚夏末示眾云。初秋夏末。兄弟東去西去。直須向萬里無寸草處去。前後下語者皆不契。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Dahui raises Dongshan's saying and reports that successive offered responses failed to accord, preserving the public testing function.

Occurrences.Kwic: 眾下語皆不契。因僧請益。復成五頌示之。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the bamboo-slat case the assembly's responses all fail to accord, after which a monk asks for instruction.

Occurrences.Kwic: 雖然「音律不差」，而「下語用字，全不可讀」，也沒有文學價值
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Allowlisted modern scholarly body prose contrasts acceptable musical regulation with unreadable wording and characters. It is retained as a provenance/control outlier, not promoted to a separate Chan sense.

Senses.PreferredTarget: look at the word or saying
Senses.Explanation: Literally, ‘look at the talk’: look at the word, saying, question, or conversational thread singled out in a record. The compound most often occurs in ‘look at the saying's head’ (看話頭), and the local wording—not an imported technical label—determines whether English says word, saying, question, or thread. The records include a monk seeking written direction because the saying he was looking at had not opened to him. They also preserve criticism: Mingben reports people calling looking at a saying ‘doing work’ and rejects their appeal to direct transmission; Yuancheng says an old hunter neither did work nor looked at a saying before answering that there was ‘no place to set a hand,’ and contrasts this with looking left and right at one's own selected saying. Another record demands, ‘if you recognize it and can say it, come out and say it—what does the end of the talk say?’ Thus the Zen deviation is an ordinary act of looking directed at actual words in recorded exchanges and itself subjected to criticism in the record.
Senses.Note: No separate sense is created for different possible English renderings of “talk” (話) in context; they are readings of the same act and object family. Exact “look at the talk” (看話) also occurs across word boundaries in ordinary prose, so only lexically coherent deployments are curated.

Occurrences.Kwic: 說著箇看話頭做工夫。遽引信心銘，謂執之失度，必入邪路。剛謂直指單傳，無如是事。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Mingben reports and criticizes calling looking at a saying ‘doing work’; the entry does not adopt that category.

Occurrences.Kwic: 因看話頭處未通，出紙求指示
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A monk requests written direction because the saying he is looking at remains unresolved.

Occurrences.Kwic: 初不做工夫、亦不看話頭，一聞恁麼舉便云無下手處
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A record explicitly says the hunter had neither done work nor looked at a saying before his reply.

Occurrences.Kwic: 識得道得出來道看話端道什麼
Occurrences.AttributionNote: A public challenge asks one who recognizes and can say it to state what the end of the talk says.
